title: Sources in, video out
hook: You give a language model three PDFs and ask for an animated explainer. How could you check that every picture renders, every sentence traces back to a page, and each visual appears exactly when the voice reaches it?

chapters.title: Five stages, one diagram
chapters.goal: The viewer can follow one source page through ingest, outline, storyboard, voice and render, and name the file each stage produces.

claims.text: Ingest turns PDFs, text and URLs into chunks.json, with one chunk per PDF page (id notes:p6) or one per 2,500 characters of text (id readme:s2).
The outline stage has the model write chapters of claims, and every claim must cite real chunk ids.
The storyboard stage has the model fill a fixed schema, one chapter at a time.
The voice stage speaks the narration with local Kokoro TTS, one sentence at a time, and the render stage uses Remotion to make one MP4 per chapter, then joins them with chapter markers.
state.json records a hash of each stage's inputs, so a command runs only what is missing or stale, and rewriting one chapter leaves the other chapters byte-identical.

chapters.title: Fill a storyboard, not code
chapters.goal: The viewer can predict, then see, that the model never writes animation code, and can read a diagram primitive's nodes, edges and steps.

claims.text: Many people expect the model to write animation code, but Emoton's model never does: it fills a declarative storyboard instead.
The README names seven primitives that always render: title, bullets, diagram, sequence, equation, code and graph.
A diagram is defined as nodes, edges and an ordered list of steps, and each step can show, hide, highlight or relabel ids.
In the README's example, step one shows the sources node and step two shows the storyboard node and the outline edge between them.
Setting continue to true keeps the previous beat's diagram on screen so the next beat builds on it.

chapters.title: Bad output goes back
chapters.goal: The viewer can say what the validator catches, why some limits are checked only afterwards, and how each claim stays tied to a source chunk.

claims.text: A validator checks every answer, and invalid output goes back to the writer along with the list of errors.
Structured-output backends support only part of JSON Schema, so the size limits are removed from the schema the writer sees, and zod still enforces every limit afterwards.
A cross-check catches what the schema cannot express, such as an edge that points at an unknown node, or continue set to true when the previous beat is not a diagram.
Every outline claim cites one to four chunk ids, and every beat can list the chunk ids that back it.
The prompt and accept commands let any writer, a person or an agent, produce the JSON, and accept runs the same validation.

chapters.title: Sentence k reveals item k
chapters.goal: The viewer can apply the one timing rule to a beat and explain why keeping visuals in sync needs no alignment model, which ties back to the opening question.

claims.text: Every primitive has an ordered list of reveal items, and item k appears when sentence k of the beat starts.
Items beyond the last sentence are spread across the last sentence.
The voice stage speaks each sentence separately, so every sentence start is known exactly and keeping the visuals in sync needs no alignment model.
The voice stage records the start and end time of each sentence in seconds, and the renderer reads those timings.

So the answer to the opening question is that primitives which always render, a validator that sends back errors, cited chunk ids and one timing rule make each part of the video something you can check.
